what: 1. rpasurvival - Recursive Partitioning Analysis for Survival Staging
title: 🎯 New Features Implemented: RPA Survival Staging & Groome Comparison
text: Location: Analyses → Survival → RPA Survival Staging Purpose: Develop risk stratification groups using binary tree partitioning survival data (CART survival). Use Case: Integrate multiple predictors (e.g., LVI + ypTNM stage) create improved prognostic groups. Key Features: - ✨ Automatic binary tree splitting using log-rank likelihood criterion - ✨ Cross-validation automatic pruning (10-fold default) - ✨ Configurable complexity parameters (minbucket, cp, maxdepth) - ✨ Multiple risk group labeling schemes (Stage -II-III, Low-High Risk, etc.) - ✨ Decision tree visualization rpart.plot - ✨ Kaplan-Meier curves risk group survminer - ✨ Hazard ratio table Cox regression - ✨ Variable importance scores - ✨ Creates new variable RPA stage assignments - ✨ Comprehensive error handling user guidance Example Output:
code: Root (n=565) ├─ ypTNM Stage I-II │  ├─ LVI Absent → RPA Stage I (n=336, 5-yr OS: 68%) │  └─ LVI Present → RPA Stage II (n=27, 5-yr OS: 40%) └─ ypTNM Stage III-IVA    ├─ LVI Absent → RPA Stage II (n=148, 5-yr OS: 49%)    └─ LVI Present → RPA Stage III (n=54, 5-yr OS: 15%)

title: 🎯 New Features Implemented: RPA Survival Staging & Groome Comparison
text: Location: Analyses → Survival → Groome Staging Comparison Purpose: Compare two staging systems using well-accepted Groome criteria (4 metrics + overall rank). Use Case: Demonstrate new staging system (e.g., RPA) superior existing system (e.g., ypTNM). Key Features: - ✨ 4 Groome Criteria calculated automatically: - Hazard Consistency (max|log(HR_i/HR_j)|) - smaller = better - Hazard Discrimination (range log(HR)) - larger = better - Sample Balance (max(n_i/n_j)) - smaller = better - Outcome Prediction (weighted combination) - smaller = better - ✨ Overall Rank determination (smaller = winner) - ✨ Winner identification percentage improvement - ✨ Detailed hazard ratio tables systems - ✨ Sample size distribution analysis - ✨ C-index comparison 95% CI - ✨ Radar chart visualization (fmsb package) - ✨ Bar chart comparison - ✨ Side--side Kaplan-Meier curves - ✨ Optional bootstrap validation (1000 replicates) Example Output:
code: Comparison Summary: ┌─────────────────────┬────────────┬───────────┬──────────────┐ │ Criterion           │ ypTNM      │ RPA Stage │ Better       │ ├─────────────────────┼────────────┼───────────┼──────────────┤ │ Hazard Consistency  │ 1.549      │ 1.451     │ RPA Stage    │ │ Hazard Discriminat. │ 1.684      │ 1.316     │ RPA Stage    │ │ Sample Balance      │ 1.998      │ 1.002     │ RPA Stage    │ │ Outcome Prediction  │ 1.745      │ 1.255     │ RPA Stage    │ │ Overall Rank        │ 7.976      │ 5.024     │ RPA Stage ✓  │ └─────────────────────┴────────────┴───────────┴──────────────┘  Winner: RPA Stage (37% better overall rank)

text: Problem: Variable names spaces/special characters caused formula errors Solution: Impact: Handles edge cases like: - Variable names spaces:                 "Survival Time (months)" → `Survival.Time..months.` - Special characters:                 "T-stage (modified)" → `T.stage..modified.` - Reserved R words:                 "class" → `class`
code: # Centralized escaping function stagemigration_escapeVar <- function(varname, backticks = TRUE) {     escaped <- make.names(varname, unique = TRUE)     escaped <- gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9_.]", "_", escaped)     if (backticks) escaped <- paste0("`", escaped, "`")     return(escaped) }  # Safe formula building old_formula <- stagemigration_buildFormula(     time_var, event_var, old_stage ) # Returns: Surv(`survival_time`, `event_binary`) ~ `old_stage`

what: Scenario 1: Right-Skewed Lab Values with Outliers
title: Single Variable Quality Check (checkdata) - Comprehensive Guide
text: Symptoms: - High skewness (>1) - Z-score flags outliers, IQR/MAD don’t - Large CV (>50%) Actions: 1. Re-run Outlier Transform: Log 2. Check outliers become consensus log scale 3. Report MAD instead SD spread 4. Use log-transformed values parametric tests Example:
code: Before log transform: - Skewness: 2.3 (severe right skew) - Outliers: 5 by Z-score, 0 by IQR/MAD - CV: 85% (very high)  After log transform: - Skewness: 0.3 (nearly symmetric) - Outliers: 2 consensus (2/3 methods on log scale) - CV: 12% (moderate)

title: Single Variable Quality Check (checkdata) - Comprehensive Guide
text: : Coefficient variation unstable mean near zero (creates large undefined ratios). what: Why Bootstrap is Correct for Dependent Samples
title: Independent vs Dependent Sampling: Statistical Implications for Pathology Adequacy Analysis
text: Key insight: Bootstrap resamples case level, block level bootstrap sample preserves within-case dependence structure:
code: Original data: 3 cases - Case A: VI first in block 1 (large, anterior invasion) - Case B: VI first in block 6 (small, posterior invasion) - Case C: VI first in block 2 (moderate, central)  Bootstrap iteration 1: [A, A, C]  # Case A sampled twice Bootstrap iteration 2: [B, C, C] Bootstrap iteration 3: [A, B, A] ...  Each iteration preserves the spatial pattern WITHIN each case. CIs reflect uncertainty about which TYPES of cases you might encounter, not uncertainty about whether block 3 is independent of block 2.

text: works: - Captures non-linear relationships - Works mixed data types - Detects patterns like “Ki67 high p53 strong positive” - Information-theoretic approach (model-free) Example Results: Clinical Decision Tree: Comparison: MI vs. Correlation:
code: ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ MUTUAL INFORMATION ANALYSIS ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════  Marker Pair: p53 (ordinal) vs Ki67 (continuous) ├─ Mutual Information = 0.62 bits ├─ Normalized MI = 0.58 (moderate information sharing) ├─ ├─ Breakdown by p53 intensity: │   p53 0/1+  : Ki67 mean = 3.2%  (σ = 2.1)  ← G1 tumors │   p53 2+    : Ki67 mean = 12.5% (σ = 5.3)  ← G2 tumors │   p53 3+    : Ki67 mean = 48.7% (σ = 18.2) ← G3 tumors │ └─ Interpretation: Strong non-linear relationship     (High p53 predicts high Ki67, but not vice versa)  Marker Pair: Chromogranin vs Ki67 ├─ Mutual Information = 0.12 bits ├─ Normalized MI = 0.08 (weak information sharing) └─ Interpretation: Independent markers     (Chromogranin doesn't predict proliferation)  Marker Pair: Chromogranin vs Synaptophysin ├─ Mutual Information = 0.78 bits ├─ Normalized MI = 0.85 (strong information sharing) ├─ Co-expression: 92% of cases └─ Interpretation: Redundant markers     (One is sufficient for NET diagnosis) Neuroendocrine Tumor Confirmation:     ├─ Chromogranin [+] ──┐     └─ Synaptophysin [+] ─┴─→ High MI (redundant)          │          → Recommendation: Use ONE for diagnosis  Grading (Non-linear pattern detected):     ├─ Ki67 < 3%  + p53 0/1+ → Grade 1 (Low-grade)     ├─ Ki67 3-20% + p53 2+   → Grade 2 (Intermediate)     └─ Ki67 > 20% + p53 3+   → Grade 3 (High-grade)          │          → Pattern: p53 intensity increases WITH Ki67          → MI detects this non-linear association          → Linear correlation would miss this pattern! Using Standard Correlation (Linear): p53 vs Ki67 correlation = 0.42 └─ Would conclude: "Moderate positive correlation"    (Misses the threshold effects!)  Using Mutual Information (Non-linear): p53 vs Ki67 normalized MI = 0.58 └─ Detects: "Strong information sharing with thresholds"    (Captures the G1/G2/G3 transition points!)  Clinical Impact: ✅ MI correctly identifies: p53 3+ predicts high Ki67 ❌ Correlation misses: The threshold nature of grading

code: Consider a 100-case dataset:  Using Chi-squared: ├─ Includes double-negatives in calculation ├─ PAX8[-]/CK7[-] cases (90 cases) → counted as "agreement" └─ Can inflate association when many negatives  Using Jaccard: ├─ Ignores double-negatives ├─ Focuses on: PAX8[+]/CK7[+] co-positivity └─ Clinically relevant: we care about positive co-expression ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ JACCARD ANALYSIS (Co-positivity Focus) ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════  Clear Cell RCC Pattern: PAX8 vs RCC marker: ├─ Both positive: 68/100 cases ├─ Either positive: 72/100 cases ├─ Jaccard Index = 68/72 = 0.94 (very high!) └─ Interpretation: Nearly always co-express in ccRCC  PAX8 vs CD10: ├─ Both positive: 65/100 cases ├─ Either positive: 70/100 cases ├─ Jaccard Index = 65/70 = 0.93 └─ Interpretation: Strong co-expression in ccRCC  PAX8 vs CK7: ├─ Both positive: 8/100 cases ├─ Either positive: 78/100 cases ├─ Jaccard Index = 8/78 = 0.10 (very low!) └─ Interpretation: Rarely co-express (mutually exclusive)  Vimentin: ├─ Positive in most RCCs (non-specific) ├─ Jaccard with others: 0.60-0.70 └─ Interpretation: Sensitive but not specific Clear Cell RCC Cluster:     PAX8 ──┬── Jaccard distance = 0.06 (nearly identical)     RCC ───┤            ├── All cluster tightly     CD10 ──┘   (co-positive in ccRCC)  Papillary RCC Pattern:     CK7 ──────── Separate (low Jaccard with ccRCC markers)  Non-specific:     Vimentin ─── Moderate distance from all RCC Subtype Differentiation: ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Clear Cell RCC:                                 │ │   PAX8[+], RCC[+], CD10[+], CK7[-], Vim[+]    │ │                                                 │ │   Marker Cluster: PAX8-RCC-CD10                │ │   └─ High Jaccard (0.93-0.94) = Redundant!     │ │                                                 │ │   Minimal Panel: PAX8 + CK7                    │ │   └─ PAX8[+]/CK7[-] → Likely ccRCC            │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Papillary RCC:                                  │ │   PAX8[+], RCC[+/-], CD10[-/+], CK7[+], Vim[+]│ │                                                 │ │   Key Discriminator: CK7                       │ │   └─ Low Jaccard with ccRCC markers (0.10)     │ │                                                 │ │   Minimal Panel: PAX8 + CK7                    │ │   └─ PAX8[+]/CK7[+] → Likely pRCC             │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  Cost Optimization: ✅ Keep: PAX8 (renal lineage), CK7 (subtype discriminator) ❌ Drop: RCC marker (redundant with PAX8, Jaccard = 0.94) ❌ Drop: CD10 (redundant with PAX8, Jaccard = 0.93) ⚠️ Optional: Vimentin (non-specific, moderate Jaccard)  Potential Savings: ├─ 2-3 antibodies per case ├─ Maintains diagnostic accuracy └─ Based on co-expression analysis

code: ❌ WRONG Approach: "CK7 and CK20 cluster together, so I'll drop CK20"  ✅ CORRECT Approach: "CK7 and CK20 cluster together. Let me check:  1. Do they truly co-express or are both negative?  2. code: library(survival)  # A minimal simulated trial: does Treatment benefit differ by Biomarker status? set.seed(1) n <- 300 dat <- data.frame(   Treatment = factor(sample(c("Control", "Drug"), n, replace = TRUE)),   Biomarker = factor(sample(c("Negative", "Positive"), n, replace = TRUE)) ) lp <- with(dat, -0.1 * (Treatment == "Drug") +                  -0.9 * (Treatment == "Drug" & Biomarker == "Positive")) dat$time  <- rexp(n, rate = exp(lp) * 0.1) dat$event <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.8)  # Treatment (focal) x Biomarker (moderator): the interaction test fit <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ Treatment * Biomarker, data = dat) summary(fit)  # Within-subgroup HR for Treatment, computed the same way multisurvival does: # relevel Biomarker to each level and re-read the Treatment coefficient. fit_neg <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ Treatment * relevel(Biomarker, ref = "Negative"), data = dat) fit_pos <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ Treatment * relevel(Biomarker, ref = "Positive"), data = dat)

title: Adaptive LASSO Cox Regression for Variable Selection in Survival Analysis
text: Adaptive LASSO Cox Regression module (adaptivelasso) performs penalized variable selection Cox proportional hazards models using data-driven adaptive weights. Unlike standard LASSO, adaptive LASSO assigns differential penalties coefficient based initial estimate importance. achieves oracle property - meaning asymptotically, selects true model true sparse structure known advance. matters practice standard LASSO can -shrink large coefficients -shrink small ones, producing biased estimates. adaptive variant corrects penalizing unimportant variables aggressively leaving truly important predictors relatively unpenalized, yielding sparser models less bias. Key capabilities: Five weight methods (ridge, univariate Cox, full Cox, marginal correlation, equal) Elastic net mixing handling correlated predictors Cross-validated lambda selection deviance C-index criteria Stability selection via bootstrap robust variable identification Proportional hazards testing influence diagnostics Risk group stratification survival predictions Six visualization types (regularization path, CV curve, stability, survival curves, baseline hazard, diagnostics)

title: Adaptive LASSO Cox Regression for Variable Selection in Survival Analysis
text: gamma parameter controls sharply adaptive weights differentiate strong weak predictors. Higher gamma gives aggressive selection. Gamma = 0.5 (Mild adaptation): Weights less extreme. variables tend survive selection. Gamma = 1.0 (Default): Standard adaptive LASSO. Gamma = 2.0 (Strong adaptation): Weights extreme. strongest predictors survive; marginal predictors aggressively excluded. Guidance: Use gamma=0.5 exploratory analysis (retain variables), gamma=1.0 default, gamma=2.0 need sparse final model. high-dimensional settings, larger gamma helps control false selections.

text: cross-validation criterion determines model optimizes lambda selection. two available measures partial likelihood deviance Harrell’s C-index. Deviance (default): Optimizes partial likelihood. standard choice computationally efficient. C-index (Harrell’s concordance): Optimizes discrimination ability - probability random pair patients, one higher risk score earlier event. focuses ranking rather calibration. Choosing deviance C-index: Use deviance (default) general-purpose model building calibration matters. Use C-index discrimination (ranking patients correctly) primary goal, prognostic risk scores.

title: Overall, Cause Specific, and Competing Survival - Comprehensive Guide
text: clinical research, patients often risk dying multiple causes. Standard Kaplan-Meier analysis treats competing events (e.g., death causes) censored observations, overestimates actual probability event interest. Competing risks methods address bias. Key concepts: Kaplan-Meier / Overall Survival: deaths events. Simple familiar, distinguish cause. Cause-Specific Survival: deaths disease interest events; competing deaths censored. Estimates cause-specific hazard can overestimate cumulative incidence. Cumulative Incidence Function (CIF): proper probability experiencing event interest presence competing risks. Always <= 1 minus KM estimate. Gray’s Test: competing-risks analog log-rank test. Compares CIF curves groups. Fine-Gray Model: Subdistribution hazard regression. Unlike cause-specific Cox, directly models CIF, making hazard ratios interpretable terms cumulative incidence.

title: Conditional Survival Estimation - Comprehensive Guide
text: clinical oncology, patient’s prognosis improves additional year disease-free survival. Standard Kaplan-Meier estimates describe probability surviving beyond time t moment diagnosis treatment. Conditional survival answers different often useful question: given patient already survived time s, probability surviving time t? Formally: CS(t | s) = P(T > t | T > s) = S(t) / S(s) implemented via conditionalsurvival() function jsurvival module (menu: SurvivalD > ClinicoPath Survival). Four estimation methods available:

title: Firth's Penalized Likelihood Regression - Comprehensive Guide
text: Firth’s penalized likelihood regression adds Jeffreys-prior penalty likelihood function, producing finite bias-corrected coefficient estimates even standard maximum likelihood fails. essential clinical studies small samples, rare events, complete/quasi-complete separation - situations standard logistic Cox regression produces infinite severely biased estimates. Unlike LASSO (selects variables shrinking zero), Firth regression keeps variables corrects first-order bias. provides profile likelihood confidence intervals (accurate Wald small samples), penalized likelihood ratio test p-values, automatic separation detection. module supports two modes: Firth logistic regression (binary outcomes via logistf package) Firth Cox regression (survival outcomes via coxphf package). reference implementations Georg Heinze.

title: Group LASSO Cox Regression - Comprehensive Guide
text: Group LASSO fits penalized Cox proportional hazards models select remove pre-defined variable groups simultaneously. Unlike standard LASSO (selects individual variables), Group LASSO uses L1/L2 mixed norm penalty group level via grpreg R package. ensures entire groups variables (e.g., dummy codes categorical variable, genes pathway, biomarkers clinical panel) selected excluded together. module supports four penalty types (Group LASSO, Group MCP, Group SCAD, Adaptive Group LASSO), multiple grouping strategies, stability selection robust variable identification, nested cross-validation unbiased performance assessment, permutation testing statistical significance. analysis particularly valuable genomic survival studies natural pathway groupings, clinical prediction models domain-based predictor sets, scenario interpretable group-wise feature selection preferred individual variable selection.

title: High-Dimensional Cox Regression - Comprehensive Guide
text: High-Dimensional Cox Regression module (highdimcox) provides unified interface regularized Cox regression number predictors large relative sample size. supports LASSO, Ridge, Elastic Net, Adaptive LASSO regularization, optional stability selection robust variable identification. module designed : Genomic survival studies (gene expression panels, mutation data) Proteomic/metabolomic data (high-dimensional biomarker panels) Radiomics studies (texture morphology features imaging) p >> n survival scenario Key features: Multiple regularization methods one interface Cross-validation configurable lambda selection (min, 1se) Stability selection via bootstrap robust variable identification Variable importance coefficient visualization Model diagnostics performance metrics Data suitability assessment traffic-light checks

title: High-Dimensional Cox Regression - Comprehensive Guide
text: predictors observations (close ), standard Cox regression fails. Regularization adds penalty prevent overfitting. Elastic Net (default, alpha=0.5) recommended starting point - combines variable selection LASSO stability Ridge.

title: High-Dimensional Cox Regression - Comprehensive Guide
text: Pure LASSO selects sparsest model - ideal expect true predictors.
code: # Simulate a genomic survival study (150 patients, 100 genes) set.seed(42) n <- 150 p_genes <- 100  # Gene expression matrix gene_matrix <- matrix(rnorm(n * p_genes), nrow = n) colnames(gene_matrix) <- paste0("GENE_", sprintf("%03d", 1:p_genes))  # True effects: 6 genes affect survival true_effects <- rep(0, p_genes) true_effects[c(5, 12, 27, 43, 68, 91)] <- c(0.8, -0.6, 0.5, -0.4, 0.7, -0.5)  # Clinical variables age <- rnorm(n, 62, 10) gender <- factor(sample(c("Male", "Female"), n, replace = TRUE)) stage <- factor(sample(c("I", "II", "III"), n,   replace = TRUE,   prob = c(0.3, 0.4, 0.3) )) grade <- factor(sample(1:3, n, replace = TRUE)) treatment <- factor(sample(c("A", "B"), n, replace = TRUE))  # Survival times lp <- gene_matrix %*% true_effects + 0.02 * (age - 62) + 0.3 * (as.numeric(stage) - 1) surv_time <- rweibull(n, shape = 1.3, scale = 30 * exp(-as.numeric(lp) * 0.2)) censor_time <- runif(n, 6, 48) time <- pmax(pmin(surv_time, censor_time), 0.1) event <- factor(ifelse(surv_time <= censor_time, "Dead", "Alive"),   levels = c("Alive", "Dead") )  data_genomic <- data.frame(   survival_months = time,   vital_status = event,   age = age, gender = gender, stage = stage,   grade = grade, treatment = treatment,   as.data.frame(gene_matrix) )  cat(   "N:", n, "Events:", sum(event == "Dead"),   "Event rate:", round(mean(event == "Dead"), 2), "\n" ) #> N: 150 Events: 90 Event rate: 0.6 cat("Predictors:", ncol(data_genomic) - 2, "\n") #> Predictors: 105 # All gene predictors (no clinical for clean LASSO demonstration) gene_vars <- paste0("GENE_", sprintf("%03d", 1:p_genes))  highdimcox(   data = data_genomic,   elapsedtime = "survival_months",   outcome = "vital_status",   outcomeLevel = "Dead",   censorLevel = "Alive",   predictors = gene_vars,   regularization_method = "lasso",   cv_method = "cv_1se",   cv_folds = 10,   show_regularization_path = TRUE,   show_cv_plot = TRUE,   show_variable_importance = TRUE,   show_coefficients_table = TRUE ) #> Error: #> ! Argument 'predictors' contains 'gene_vars' which is not present in the dataset

title: High-Dimensional Cox Regression - Comprehensive Guide
text: Using Ridge need variable selection: Ridge never sets coefficients exactly zero. interpretable models, use LASSO Elastic Net. adjusting CV folds small samples: n < 100, use cv_folds = 5 instead 10 ensure adequate events per fold. Ignoring stability selection: single regularized model may give unstable variable selections. Use stability selection (subsampling_iterations >= 200) robust results. Comparing models different alpha values: Models different alpha values optimize different objectives. Compare using alpha use nested cross-validation. reporting regularization method: Always report method (LASSO/Ridge/Elastic Net), alpha value, CV method, number selected variables. Training C-index overestimates performance: reported C-index computed training data optimistically biased. Always validate external data clinical use.

title: LASSO Cox Regression for Variable Selection in Survival Analysis
text: Lasso-Cox Regression module (lassocox) performs automatic variable selection survival analysis using L1-penalized Cox proportional hazards regression. identifies important predictors preventing overfitting - ideal clinicopathological research many candidate variables. Key features: Data suitability assessment (traffic-light system) Cross-validated lambda selection (lambda.min vs lambda.1se) Variable selection coefficient shrinkage Risk score calculation patient stratification Comprehensive visualizations (CV plot, coefficient plot, survival curves) Clinical interpretation guidance

title: LASSO Cox Regression for Variable Selection in Survival Analysis
text: LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage Selection Operator) Cox regression combines Cox proportional hazards model L1 regularization automatic variable selection. Standard Cox model: h(t)=h0(t)exp⁡(β1x1+β2x2+⋯+βpxp)h(t) = h_0(t) \exp(\beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p) LASSO Cox adds penalty: Maximize:ℓ(β)−λ∑j=1p|βj|\text{Maximize:} \quad \ell(\beta) - \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j| ℓ(β)\ell(\beta) partial log-likelihood λ\lambda controls penalty strength. effect: small coefficients shrink toward zero, irrelevant variables become exactly zero, important predictors remain model.

previous_headings: LASSO Cox Regression > Common Pitfalls and Best Practices
title: LASSO Cox Regression for Variable Selection in Survival Analysis
text: Using LASSO events: EPV < 2 produces unreliable results. Even regularization, LASSO needs sufficient events - common problem small radiomics cohorts (e.g., 80 patients 300 features). standardizing variables: LASSO sensitive scale. variable measured 0 - 20,000 (e.g., tumor area) dominate one measured 0 - 100 (e.g., age) unless standardized. Use standardize = TRUE (default). Interpreting coefficients p-values: LASSO performs selection, testing. Incorrect: “LASSO identified Ki67 statistically significant.” Correct: “LASSO selected Ki67 important predictor.” Feature selection full data (data leakage): common mistake. perform LASSO feature selection patients, build test model data, information leaks test set selection step. Feature selection must done within training set . external validation: Internal cross-validation produces optimistically biased estimates. Journals increasingly require external validation cohorts. validation hierarchy: Internal cross-validation (minimum) Internal train/test split External independent dataset (preferred) Ignoring feature stability: Radiomic WSI features may change scanner, staining protocol, segmentation method, resolution. LASSO, features tested robustness using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) test - retest analysis. Reporting selected variables: Good reporting requires: selected features, lambda value used, cross-validation method, coefficient values, performance metrics. Follow TRIPOD statement transparent reporting. Ignoring clinical variables: radiomics papers include image features. Combined models (clinical + pathological + radiomic + molecular) usually perform better. assessing model performance properly: Survival models report C-index calibration curves. High discrimination (C-index) alone insufficient - model must also well-calibrated. Consider decision curve analysis clinical utility. calibration analysis: model high AUC/C-index poor calibration makes systematically wrong predictions. Always check calibration plots consider Hosmer-Lemeshow test calibration slope.

title: SCAD/MCP Cox Regression for Variable Selection in Survival Analysis
text: SCAD/MCP Cox Regression module (ncvregcox) performs variable selection using non-convex penalties - SCAD (Smoothly Clipped Absolute Deviation) MCP (Minimax Concave Penalty) - Cox proportional hazards models. penalties solve fundamental problem LASSO: -penalization large coefficients. Key features: Two non-convex penalty types: SCAD MCP Oracle properties: Consistent selection + unbiased estimation large effects Data suitability assessment (traffic-light system 6 checks) Cross-validated lambda selection (min 1-SE rule) Regularization path visualization Variable importance analysis

title: SCAD/MCP Cox Regression for Variable Selection in Survival Analysis
text: LASSO applies constant penalty rate regardless coefficient size, means: Small (noise) coefficients: shrunk zero (good) Large (true) coefficients: also -shrunk (bad - introduces bias) SCAD MCP use penalties flatten large coefficients, solving problem. key insight coefficient clearly non-zero, reason keep penalizing .

title: SCAD/MCP Cox Regression for Variable Selection in Survival Analysis
text: SCAD penalty (Fan & Li, 2001): P(β)={λ|β||β|≤λ−(β2−2γλ|β|+λ2)2(γ−1)λ<|β|≤γλ(γ+1)λ22if |β|>γλP(\beta) = \begin{cases} \lambda |\beta| & \text{} |\beta| \leq \lambda \\ \frac{-(\beta^2 - 2\gamma\lambda|\beta| + \lambda^2)}{2(\gamma-1)} & \text{} \lambda < |\beta| \leq \gamma\lambda \\ \frac{(\gamma+1)\lambda^2}{2} & \text{} |\beta| > \gamma\lambda \end{cases} MCP (Zhang, 2010): P(β)={λ|β|−β22γif |β|≤γλγλ22if |β|>γλP(\beta) = \begin{cases} \lambda |\beta| - \frac{\beta^2}{2\gamma} & \text{} |\beta| \leq \gamma\lambda \\ \frac{\gamma\lambda^2}{2} & \text{} |\beta| > \gamma\lambda \end{cases} default γ=3.7\gamma = 3.7 SCAD recommended Fan & Li (2001) based Bayesian arguments minimization Bayesian risk. MCP, recommended default γ=3.0\gamma = 3.0 (Zhang, 2010). penalties behave like LASSO near zero (good eliminating noise) stop penalizing coefficients exceed threshold γλ\gamma\lambda. two-regime behavior gives oracle property: regularity conditions, select correct model estimate non-zero coefficients true model known advance.

title: SCAD/MCP Cox Regression for Variable Selection in Survival Analysis
text: gamma parameter controls quickly penalty flattens: SCAD: gamma must > 2. Default 3.7 (Fan & Li recommendation) MCP: gamma must > 1. Default 3.0. Lower gamma = aggressive selection Interpretation: gamma increases, SCAD behaves like LASSO (constant penalty rate). gamma decreases toward 2, SCAD becomes aggressive removing penalty large coefficients. default 3.7 well-studied compromise.

text: cross-validation procedure identifies optimal penalty strength (lambda). Two strategies available: min: Lambda minimizes CV error - selects variables 1se: Lambda within 1 SE minimum - parsimonious (Breiman’s rule) Practical tip: 1-SE model drops variable consider clinically important, inspect CV error plot. two lambda values close, difference likely within noise. far apart, 1-SE model genuinely simpler may generalize better.

title: PLS Cox Regression for High-Dimensional Survival Analysis
text: PLS Cox Regression module (plscox) combines Partial Least Squares (PLS) dimensionality reduction Cox proportional hazards modeling high-dimensional survival data. Instead selecting individual variables like LASSO, PLS creates latent components - weighted combinations predictors maximally explain covariance survival outcome. Key features: Component selection via cross-validation (log-likelihood, C-index), information criteria (BIC, AIC), manual Multiple scaling methods (standardization, unit variance, min-max, none) Advanced PLS settings (sparse PLS, Q-squared stopping, p-value variable selection) Bootstrap validation (Harrell optimism-corrected C-index) Permutation testing overall model significance Risk group stratification Kaplan-Meier survival curves Variable importance (Cox-weighted PLS loadings) Data suitability assessment (traffic-light system 6 checks)

title: PLS Cox Regression for High-Dimensional Survival Analysis
text: Use PLS : - Variables highly correlated (metabolomics, gene expression) - want retain information variables - underlying signal comes latent biological processes - p >> n LASSO produces unstable selections Use LASSO : - want identify individual important predictors - sparse, interpretable model needed - Variables relatively independent

title: PLS Cox Regression for High-Dimensional Survival Analysis
text: many components: components can mean overfitting. Always use cross-validation select optimal number. Ignoring variable scaling: Metabolites different scales dominate PLS standardized. Always use scaling_method = "standardize" (default). validating: Use bootstrap validation /permutation testing assess reliability. training C-index overestimates true performance. Interpreting loadings independent effects: high loading means variable contributes component, independent causal effect. Groups correlated variables share loading magnitude. Using LOO CV large datasets: Leave-one-computationally expensive can unstable. Use 5- 10-fold CV n > 50. Sparse PLS components: Sparse PLS may return NULL component scores configurations. happens, try increasing components disabling sparse mode.

title: Relative Survival Analysis - Comprehensive Guide
text: Relative survival analysis compares observed survival patient cohort survival expected matched general population. Rather requiring (often inaccurate) cause--death data, estimates disease-specific mortality indirectly ratio observed expected survival. approach standard population-based cancer epidemiology used EUROCARE, CONCORD, national cancer registries worldwide. relativesurvival module provides: Four estimation methods: Pohar-Perme (recommended), Ederer , Ederer II, Hakulinen 15 population rate tables: 4 relsurv package (US, Minnesota, France, Slovenia) 10 -based tables (Turkey, Germany, UK, Italy, Japan, Spain, Brazil, South Korea, China, India), plus custom option Net survival excess mortality estimation Crude probability death decomposition (disease vs. causes) ICSS age standardization international comparisons Period analysis track survival trends diagnosis years Regression models: additive excess hazard, multiplicative, flexible parametric (via rstpm2) Four publication-ready plots: observed, expected, relative survival, excess mortality

text: survival function ClinicoPath provides comprehensive suite survival analysis tools designed clinicopathological research. combines Kaplan-Meier estimation, Cox proportional hazards regression, wide range advanced methods single, unified analysis. produces default (optional flags needed): Median survival time 95% confidence intervals group Cox proportional hazards regression hazard ratios Survival probability table user-specified time points (default: 12, 36, 60 months) can add single checkbox: Kaplan-Meier plots, cumulative events/hazard plots, KMunicate-style plots Pairwise group comparisons multiple testing correction Proportional hazards assumption testing Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) Person-time analysis incidence rates Weighted log-rank tests (Fleming-Harrington family) Bootstrap internal validation (optimism-corrected C-index) Calibration curves Cox model assessment Non-linearity assessment via restricted cubic splines Age-adjusted, age-stratified, age--time-scale models Competing risks cause-specific survival REMARK reporting checklist Natural language summaries clinical interpretation Clinical safety features: Analysis blocked fewer 10 events detected Warnings issued low event counts (10-19, 20-49) Competing risk mode automatically skips analyses valid context

title: Enhanced ROC Analysis for Clinical Biomarker Evaluation
text: Enhanced ROC Analysis module (timeroc) evaluates well continuous biomarkers predict clinical outcomes. provides dual-mode architecture: Time-Dependent ROC (via timeROC package): Evaluates marker performance specific timepoints using cumulative/dynamic ROC curves Inverse Probability Censoring Weights (IPCW). General Binary ROC (via pROC package): Standard diagnostic ROC binary classification without time component. Key capabilities: IPCW weighting methods: Kaplan-Meier (marginal), Cox model, Aalen additive Asymptotic confidence intervals via influence functions Optimal cutoff calculation using Youden index Multi-marker comparison DeLong, Bootstrap, Venkatraman tests Clinical interpretation severity-graded notices

title: Latent biomarker constructs and survival
text: Clinical research regularly confronts frustrating mismatch: biological process care genuinely latent - single measurement - yet survival model needs one number per patient compute hazard ratio. Examples abound. Immune phenotype - tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte counts (CD8+, FoxP3+, PD-L1 combined positive score, CD68+ macrophages) partial, noisy windows onto underlying construct: hot cold immune microenvironment . Using single marker Cox covariate throws others away inflates problem multiple comparisons. Histologic aggressiveness - tumor budding count, worst pattern invasion, perineural invasion rate, lymphovascular invasion imperfect indicators aggressively carcinoma progressing. single latent “aggressiveness” factor captures shared variance discarding measurement noise. Stromal activation - α-SMA expression, collagen density, FAP+ fibroblast fraction, stiffness proxy scores digital image analysis collectively describe activated desmoplastic stroma. None ground truth; together triangulate one construct. latentbiomarker handles fitting single-factor reflective confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) lavaan, extracting factor scores, passing Cox proportional-hazards model survival. estimator switches automatically MLR (continuous indicators) WLSMV polychoric correlations (ordinal binary indicators).

text: immunophenotyping studies, pathologists score five six markers continuous near-continuous scales: CD8+ TIL density (cells/mm²), PD-L1 combined positive score (%), CD68+ macrophage fraction (%), FoxP3+ Treg density, LAG-3+ cell density. imperfect measurements one shared construct - immune activation - inter-correlations arise partly driven latent state. simulation creates 400 patients whose five markers generated single latent factor F plus independent measurement noise. mimics true data-generating process reflective model. set.seed(3) reproducibility, run latentbiomarker using MLR estimator (default -continuous indicators). MLR maximum likelihood robust Huber - White standard errors, appropriate multivariate normality assumption perfectly met - typical right-skewed IHC counts. standardised loadings fall within roughly ±0.10 true values (0.65-0.80). Cox model recovers protective HR 1.0, consistent simulated truth. CFI 0.95 RMSEA 0.06 confirm good single-factor fit - ideal happy path.
code:
set.seed(3) n <- 400  # True factor loadings for five immune markers lambda <- c(0.75, 0.70, 0.80, 0.65, 0.72)  # Latent immune factor (standardised) F <- rnorm(n)  # Unique variances: 1 - lambda^2 (reflective model) E <- sapply(sqrt(1 - lambda^2), function(sd) rnorm(n, 0, sd))  # Observed indicators matrix X <- outer(F, lambda) + E colnames(X) <- c("cd8_til", "pdl1_cps", "cd68_frac", "foxp3_density", "lag3_cells")  # Survival outcome: higher immune activation (F) -> better OS # Baseline hazard corresponds roughly to median OS 36 months set.seed(42) log_hr_true <- -0.4   # protective effect of immune activation T_surv <- rexp(n, rate = exp(log_hr_true * F) / 36) C_surv <- rexp(n, rate = 1 / 60)   # censoring around 60 months time <- pmin(T_surv, C_surv) event <- as.integer(T_surv <= C_surv)  df_scenario1 <- data.frame(X, time = time, event = event) cat("n =", n, "| events =", sum(event), "| event rate =",     round(mean(event), 2), "
") ## n = 400 | events = 238 | event rate = 0.6 # Verify the CFA recovers loadings close to truth using lavaan directly. # This is exactly what latentbiomarker calls internally. if (requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE)) {   model_syn <- '     F =~ cd8_til + pdl1_cps + cd68_frac + foxp3_density + lag3_cells   '   fit1 <- lavaan::cfa(model_syn, data = df_scenario1, estimator = "MLR",                       std.lv = TRUE)   loadings1 <- lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit1, standardized = TRUE)   loadings1 <- loadings1[loadings1$op == "=~",                           c("lhs", "rhs", "std.all", "se", "pvalue")]   names(loadings1) <- c("Factor", "Indicator", "Std_Loading", "SE", "p")   print(loadings1, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)    # Fit indices   fi <- lavaan::fitMeasures(fit1, c("cfi.robust", "tli.robust",                                     "rmsea.robust", "srmr"))   cat("
Fit indices (MLR):
")   print(round(fi, 3)) } ##  Factor     Indicator Std_Loading    SE p ##       F       cd8_til       0.778 0.045 0 ##       F      pdl1_cps       0.672 0.045 0 ##       F     cd68_frac       0.788 0.047 0 ##       F foxp3_density       0.630 0.051 0 ##       F    lag3_cells       0.699 0.050 0 ##  ## Fit indices (MLR): ##   cfi.robust   tli.robust rmsea.robust         srmr  ##        0.999        0.997        0.023        0.015 # Factor score extraction + Cox regression - the second stage if (requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE)) {   scores1 <- lavaan::lavPredict(fit1, method = "regression")[, 1]   scores1_std <- as.numeric(scale(scores1))    cox1 <- survival::coxph(     survival::Surv(time, event) ~ scores1_std,     data = df_scenario1   )   summary_cox1 <- summary(cox1)   cat("Cox HR for latent immune factor (per SD):
")   print(round(summary_cox1$coefficients[, c(1, 2, 3, 5)], 3))   cat("
True log-HR was", log_hr_true,       "| Estimated log-HR =",       round(coef(cox1), 3), "
") } ## Cox HR for latent immune factor (per SD): ##      coef exp(coef)  se(coef)  Pr(>|z|)  ##    -0.306     0.737     0.073     0.000  ##  ## True log-HR was -0.4 | Estimated log-HR = -0.306

title: Latent biomarker constructs and survival
text: IHC scoring surgical pathology almost never continuous. Pathologists routinely assign semi-quantitative scores: 0 (absent), 1+ (weak/focal), 2+ (moderate/diffuse), 3+ (strong/diffuse). four-level ordinal scale common PD-L1 tumor proportion score bins, p53 aberrant expression, chromatin pattern descriptors. indicator five fewer distinct ordered levels, Pearson correlations biased assume normality around observed values. correct association measure polychoric correlation - Pearson correlation two hypothesised underlying continuous latent responses. lavaan handles automatically ordered = TRUE specified, switches WLSMV (weighted least-squares means variance adjusted) estimation, recommended estimator ordinal manifest variables. latentbiomarker auto-detects ordinal indicators issues STRONG_WARNING notice reminding users factor loadings now latent-response scale (observed 0-3 scale) fit indices slightly different reference distributions WLSMV. Notice loadings labelled “latent-response scale.” use WLSMV, lavaan works thresholds polychoric correlations; loadings describe latent continuous response underlying score moves latent factor, observed 0 - 3 integer moves. distinction matters interpretation: loading 0.68 means one SD increase immune activation associated 0.68 SD shift latent PD-L1 response, turn shifts probabilities observable 0/1/2/3 categories via estimated thresholds.
code:
set.seed(7) n2 <- 350  # Latent immune factor (standardised) F2 <- rnorm(n2) lambda2 <- c(0.70, 0.68, 0.73, 0.65)  # Continuous underlying responses E2 <- sapply(sqrt(1 - lambda2^2), function(sd) rnorm(n2, 0, sd)) Y2_cont <- outer(F2, lambda2) + E2  # Discretise to 0/1/2/3 using quantile thresholds (produces realistic ordinal) ordinalise <- function(x, thresholds = c(-0.8, 0.2, 1.0)) {   cut(x, c(-Inf, thresholds, Inf), labels = FALSE) - 1L } X2 <- apply(Y2_cont, 2, ordinalise) colnames(X2) <- c("pdl1_score", "p53_score", "ki67_score", "her2_score")  # Survival: higher factor -> shorter OS (aggressive tumour phenotype) log_hr_true2 <- 0.35 T2 <- rexp(n2, rate = exp(log_hr_true2 * F2) / 48) C2 <- rexp(n2, rate = 1 / 72) time2 <- pmin(T2, C2) event2 <- as.integer(T2 <= C2)  df_scenario2 <- data.frame(as.data.frame(X2), time = time2, event = event2) cat("Indicator value ranges:
") ## Indicator value ranges: print(apply(X2, 2, table)) ##   pdl1_score p53_score ki67_score her2_score ## 0         76        64         78         62 ## 1        121       137        123        138 ## 2         90       104         90         90 ## 3         63        45         59         60 if (requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE)) {   # Declare indicators as ordered - this triggers polychoric correlations   # and WLSMV estimation automatically   model_ord <- '     F =~ pdl1_score + p53_score + ki67_score + her2_score   '   fit2 <- lavaan::cfa(model_ord, data = df_scenario2, estimator = "WLSMV",                       ordered = c("pdl1_score", "p53_score",                                   "ki67_score", "her2_score"),                       std.lv = TRUE)    loadings2 <- lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit2, standardized = TRUE)   loadings2 <- loadings2[loadings2$op == "=~",                           c("rhs", "std.all", "se", "pvalue")]   names(loadings2) <- c("Indicator", "Std_Loading_latent_response",                         "SE", "p")   print(loadings2, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)    fi2 <- lavaan::fitMeasures(fit2, c("cfi.robust", "tli.robust",                                      "rmsea.robust", "srmr.robust"))   cat("
Fit indices (WLSMV):
")   print(round(fi2, 3)) } ##   Indicator Std_Loading_latent_response    SE p ##  pdl1_score                       0.732 0.046 0 ##   p53_score                       0.588 0.054 0 ##  ki67_score                       0.655 0.047 0 ##  her2_score                       0.655 0.051 0 ##  ## Fit indices (WLSMV): ##   cfi.robust   tli.robust rmsea.robust  ##        1.000        1.014        0.000

what: Scenario 3 - Mixed continuous + ordinal + binary indicators
title: Latent biomarker constructs and survival
text: Real tissue microarray (TMA) whole-slide analysis datasets often combine assay types. might : CD8+ TIL density digital image analysis (continuous, cells/mm²), PD-L1 combined positive score (continuous, 0 - 100%), IHC H-score converted 0/1+/2+/3+ bin (ordinal), binary call mismatch repair deficiency (MMRd: 0 = proficient, 1 = deficient). four reflect immune microenvironment state; four worth combining. indicator non-continuous, latentbiomarker falls back WLSMV across indicators. Continuous indicators treated normally distributed, ordinal binary indicators use respective polychoric tetrachoric correlations. binary indicator mathematically two-level ordered variable - tetrachoric correlation special case polychoric. need anything special: auto-detection handles . key takeaway: can mix assay types freely long every indicator reflects construct. estimator choice driven weakest-scale indicator - even one indicator ordinal binary, WLSMV used . conservative correct. four indicators continuous, MLR preferred.
code:
set.seed(11) n3 <- 300 F3 <- rnorm(n3) lambda3 <- c(0.72, 0.68, 0.65, 0.58)   # two continuous, one ordinal, one binary  E3 <- sapply(sqrt(1 - lambda3^2), function(sd) rnorm(n3, 0, sd)) Y3_cont <- outer(F3, lambda3) + E3  # Indicators: # 1. cd8_density: continuous (cells/mm^2 on approximate scale, non-negative) cd8_density <- exp(Y3_cont[, 1] + 3)   # lognormal, strictly positive # 2. pdl1_cps: continuous (0-100) pdl1_cps <- pmax(0, pmin(100, Y3_cont[, 2] * 20 + 30)) # 3. ihc_score: ordinal 0/1/2/3 ihc_score <- cut(Y3_cont[, 3], c(-Inf, -0.7, 0.2, 0.9, Inf),                  labels = FALSE) - 1L # 4. mmrd: binary (MMR-deficient vs proficient) mmrd <- as.integer(Y3_cont[, 4] > 0.3)  # Survival log_hr3 <- -0.30 T3 <- rexp(n3, rate = exp(log_hr3 * F3) / 42) C3 <- rexp(n3, rate = 1 / 60) time3 <- pmin(T3, C3) event3 <- as.integer(T3 <= C3)  df_scenario3 <- data.frame(   cd8_density, pdl1_cps, ihc_score, mmrd,   time = time3, event = event3 )  cat("Variable types and ranges:
") ## Variable types and ranges: cat(" cd8_density: continuous, range", round(range(cd8_density)), "
") ##  cd8_density: continuous, range 2 353 cat(" pdl1_cps:    continuous, range", round(range(pdl1_cps)), "
") ##  pdl1_cps:    continuous, range 0 84 cat(" ihc_score:   ordinal, levels", sort(unique(ihc_score)), "
") ##  ihc_score:   ordinal, levels 0 1 2 3 cat(" mmrd:        binary, n(0)=", sum(mmrd == 0),     "n(1)=", sum(mmrd == 1), "
") ##  mmrd:        binary, n(0)= 187 n(1)= 113 if (requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE)) {   model_mix <- '     F =~ cd8_density + pdl1_cps + ihc_score + mmrd   '   # WLSMV required because ihc_score and mmrd are non-continuous   fit3 <- lavaan::cfa(model_mix, data = df_scenario3,                       estimator = "WLSMV",                       ordered = c("ihc_score", "mmrd"),                       std.lv = TRUE)    loadings3 <- lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit3, standardized = TRUE)   loadings3 <- loadings3[loadings3$op == "=~",                           c("rhs", "std.all", "se", "pvalue")]   names(loadings3) <- c("Indicator", "Std_Loading", "SE", "p")   print(loadings3, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE) } ##    Indicator Std_Loading    SE p ##  cd8_density       0.711 2.423 0 ##     pdl1_cps       0.531 1.120 0 ##    ihc_score       0.682 0.048 0 ##         mmrd       0.598 0.048 0

title: Latent biomarker constructs and survival
text: Small cohorts norm many specialised pathology studies: rare tumour types, TMA series single institution, pilot studies larger grants. Researchers sometimes tempted run CFA 50-80 cases specimens available. latentbiomarker refuses G1 hard gate. refusal message explains gate exists - factor loadings fit indices known unstable n = 100, standard errors substantially inflated, model convergence erratic - offers two constructive alternatives: simple z-score composite (compute indicator’s z-score, average , use Cox covariate) waiting larger cohort. z-score composite measurement model - makes claim indicators exchangeable loadings equal - defensible, transparent, reproducible way combine information small samples. cohort grows n >= 100 (ideally n >= 200), CFA approach becomes appropriate can applied retrospectively test whether loadings actually equal .
code:
set.seed(99) n4 <- 50   # too small for CFA  F4 <- rnorm(n4) lambda4 <- c(0.72, 0.68, 0.65) E4 <- sapply(sqrt(1 - lambda4^2), function(sd) rnorm(n4, 0, sd)) X4 <- outer(F4, lambda4) + E4 colnames(X4) <- c("marker_a", "marker_b", "marker_c")  time4 <- rexp(n4, rate = 1/36) event4 <- rbinom(n4, 1, 0.6)  df_scenario4 <- data.frame(as.data.frame(X4), time = time4, event = event4)  # Simulate the G1 gate check that latentbiomarker performs g1_threshold <- 100 n_obs <- nrow(df_scenario4) if (n_obs < g1_threshold) {   cat("HARD REFUSAL - G1 triggered:
")   cat("SEM is data-hungry. With n =", n_obs, "< 100,
",       "factor loadings and fit indices are unreliable.
",       "Consider:
",       "  (1) a simpler z-score composite with conventional Cox regression, or
",       "  (2) waiting for a larger cohort.
") } ## HARD REFUSAL - G1 triggered: ## SEM is data-hungry. With n = 50 < 100, ##  factor loadings and fit indices are unreliable. ##  Consider: ##    (1) a simpler z-score composite with conventional Cox regression, or ##    (2) waiting for a larger cohort. # The recommended alternative: z-score composite # For n=50, this is statistically defensible where CFA is not zscore_composite <- rowMeans(scale(df_scenario4[, c("marker_a",                                                       "marker_b",                                                       "marker_c")]))  if (requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE)) {   cox_composite <- survival::coxph(     survival::Surv(time4, event4) ~ zscore_composite,     data = df_scenario4   )   cat("Z-score composite Cox (n=50, 3 indicators):
")   print(round(summary(cox_composite)$coefficients[, c(1, 2, 5)], 3)) } ## Z-score composite Cox (n=50, 3 indicators): ##      coef exp(coef)  Pr(>|z|)  ##     0.052     1.053     0.803

what: Scenario 5 - Just-identified model with exactly 3 indicators
title: Latent biomarker constructs and survival
text: Three indicators one latent factor minimum identified CFA model, sits zero degrees freedom. means model just-identified: can reproduce observed correlations perfectly construction, regardless whether single-factor model actually correct. consequence: CFI = 1.000 TLI ≈ 1.000 definition (sign good fit) RMSEA = 0.000 (similarly uninformative) SRMR = 0.000 near zero perfect-looking indices meaningless. residual variance model-implied correlations assess model exactly many free parameters unique covariances. distinguish perfect single-factor model perfect correlated-uniqueness model. latentbiomarker issues G3-soft INFO notice exactly 3 indicators supplied, explaining structural limitation recommending users either add fourth indicator gain least 1 df, interpret results without relying fit statistics. Notice fit indices trivially perfect. bug software sign model correct - algebraic inevitability. Cox regression stage still runs HR estimate valid, make claims model fit quality. adding fourth indicator feasible, consider framing latent variable three-item composite acknowledge identification constraint explicitly methods section.
code:
set.seed(21) n5 <- 280   # adequate sample size, but only 3 indicators F5 <- rnorm(n5) lambda5 <- c(0.75, 0.70, 0.68)  E5 <- sapply(sqrt(1 - lambda5^2), function(sd) rnorm(n5, 0, sd)) X5 <- outer(F5, lambda5) + E5 colnames(X5) <- c("biomarker_1", "biomarker_2", "biomarker_3")  time5 <- rexp(n5, rate = exp(-0.25 * F5) / 40) event5 <- rbinom(n5, 1, 0.55) df_scenario5 <- data.frame(as.data.frame(X5), time = time5, event = event5)  if (requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE)) {   model5 <- '     F =~ biomarker_1 + biomarker_2 + biomarker_3   '   fit5 <- lavaan::cfa(model5, data = df_scenario5, estimator = "MLR",                       std.lv = TRUE)    cat("Model degrees of freedom:", lavaan::fitMeasures(fit5, "df"), "
")    fi5 <- lavaan::fitMeasures(fit5, c("cfi.robust", "tli.robust",                                       "rmsea.robust", "srmr"))   cat("
Fit indices (3 indicators, df = 0):
")   print(round(fi5, 3))    cat("
G3-soft INFO notice:
")   cat("With 3 indicators and 1 factor, the model is just-identified (df = 0).
",       "CFI, RMSEA, and SRMR are not meaningful - perfect fit is guaranteed
",       "by construction. Add a fourth indicator to obtain an over-identified
",       "model with testable fit.
") } ## Model degrees of freedom: 0  ##  ## Fit indices (3 indicators, df = 0): ##   cfi.robust   tli.robust rmsea.robust         srmr  ##           NA           NA            0            0  ##  ## G3-soft INFO notice: ## With 3 indicators and 1 factor, the model is just-identified (df = 0). ##  CFI, RMSEA, and SRMR are not meaningful - perfect fit is guaranteed ##  by construction. Add a fourth indicator to obtain an over-identified ##  model with testable fit.

what: Scenario 6 - Two-factor reality forced into one factor
title: Latent biomarker constructs and survival
text: Perhaps practically important failure mode running single-factor model indicators actually belong two distinct constructs. Consider panel mixes proliferative markers (Ki-67 LI, PCNA expression, Cyclin D1 expression) invasion markers (MMP-9 expression, E-cadherin loss, neural invasion extent). two groups reflect different biological processes. inter-group correlations modest; within-group correlations high. Forcing six single-factor CFA produces poor fit: CFI drops 0.95 RMSEA rises 0.10. latentbiomarker function detects via Fit-poor gate issues notice recommending SEMLj multi-factor SEM, supports correlated factors full structural model including survival. scenario illustrates Fit-poor gate useful diagnostic rather merely error condition. function refuse run - runs, reports poor fit, tells next. CFI / RMSEA flags signal forcing biological reality richer one factor single-factor straitjacket. KM plot HR may still useful summary, interpreted knowing single factor blend two distinct processes rather clean measurement one.
code:
set.seed(33) n6 <- 450  # Factor 1: proliferation F1 <- rnorm(n6) # Factor 2: invasion, moderately correlated with F1 F2 <- 0.3 * F1 + sqrt(1 - 0.3^2) * rnorm(n6)  # Loadings for each factor's three indicators l1 <- c(0.80, 0.75, 0.72)   # proliferative markers l2 <- c(0.78, 0.73, 0.70)   # invasion markers  # Residual SDs sd1 <- sqrt(1 - l1^2) sd2 <- sqrt(1 - l2^2)  # Generate indicators (independent per-column residual noise so the covariance # stays full-rank / positive-definite; matches the pattern used in scenario 4) proliferative <- outer(F1, l1) + sapply(sd1, function(s) rnorm(n6, 0, s)) invasion      <- outer(F2, l2) + sapply(sd2, function(s) rnorm(n6, 0, s))  colnames(proliferative) <- c("ki67_li", "pcna_expr", "cyclind1_expr") colnames(invasion)      <- c("mmp9_expr", "ecadherin_loss", "ni_extent")  # Survival outcome driven mainly by invasion (F2), weakly by proliferation log_hr6 <- 0.4 * F2 + 0.15 * F1 T6 <- rexp(n6, rate = exp(log_hr6) / 48) C6 <- rexp(n6, rate = 1 / 72) time6 <- pmin(T6, C6) event6 <- as.integer(T6 <= C6)  df_scenario6 <- data.frame(   as.data.frame(proliferative),   as.data.frame(invasion),   time = time6, event = event6 )  cat("Within-group correlations (proliferative):
") ## Within-group correlations (proliferative): print(round(cor(proliferative), 2)) ##               ki67_li pcna_expr cyclind1_expr ## ki67_li          1.00      0.60          0.62 ## pcna_expr        0.60      1.00          0.59 ## cyclind1_expr    0.62      0.59          1.00 cat("
Within-group correlations (invasion):
") ##  ## Within-group correlations (invasion): print(round(cor(invasion), 2)) ##                mmp9_expr ecadherin_loss ni_extent ## mmp9_expr           1.00           0.63      0.59 ## ecadherin_loss      0.63           1.00      0.51 ## ni_extent           0.59           0.51      1.00 cat("
Cross-group correlations (proliferative vs invasion):
") ##  ## Cross-group correlations (proliferative vs invasion): print(round(cor(proliferative, invasion), 2)) ##               mmp9_expr ecadherin_loss ni_extent ## ki67_li            0.16           0.19      0.19 ## pcna_expr          0.15           0.12      0.13 ## cyclind1_expr      0.14           0.16      0.12 if (requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE)) {   # Force a single-factor model across all 6 indicators   model6_single <- '     F =~ ki67_li + pcna_expr + cyclind1_expr +          mmp9_expr + ecadherin_loss + ni_extent   '   fit6_single <- lavaan::cfa(model6_single, data = df_scenario6,                               estimator = "MLR", std.lv = TRUE)    fi6_single <- lavaan::fitMeasures(fit6_single,                                      c("cfi.robust", "tli.robust",                                        "rmsea.robust", "srmr"))   cat("Single-factor model fit indices:
")   print(round(fi6_single, 3))    cfi_val  <- round(fi6_single["cfi.robust"], 3)   rmsea_val <- round(fi6_single["rmsea.robust"], 3)    if (cfi_val < 0.95 || rmsea_val > 0.10) {     cat("
Fit-poor notice (as shown in latentbiomarker):
")     cat("Single-factor model fits poorly (CFI =", cfi_val,         ", RMSEA =", rmsea_val, ").
",         "Consider splitting into multiple constructs.
",         "SEMLj supports multi-factor SEM with survival outcomes.
")   } } ## Single-factor model fit indices: ##   cfi.robust   tli.robust rmsea.robust         srmr  ##        0.566        0.276        0.317        0.197  ##  ## Fit-poor notice (as shown in latentbiomarker): ## Single-factor model fits poorly (CFI = 0.566 , RMSEA = 0.317 ). ##  Consider splitting into multiple constructs. ##  SEMLj supports multi-factor SEM with survival outcomes. if (requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE)) {   # Compare with the correct two-factor model for reference   model6_correct <- '     Proliferation =~ ki67_li + pcna_expr + cyclind1_expr     Invasion      =~ mmp9_expr + ecadherin_loss + ni_extent     Proliferation ~~ Invasion   '   fit6_correct <- lavaan::cfa(model6_correct, data = df_scenario6,                                estimator = "MLR", std.lv = TRUE)    fi6_correct <- lavaan::fitMeasures(fit6_correct,                                       c("cfi.robust", "tli.robust",                                         "rmsea.robust", "srmr"))   cat("Two-factor model fit indices (for comparison - requires SEMLj):
")   print(round(fi6_correct, 3))    cat("
Conclusion: The two-factor model fits well (CFI >= 0.95, RMSEA <= 0.06),
",       "while the single-factor model does not. The Fit-poor diagnostic correctly
",       "invites users to graduate to multi-factor SEM in SEMLj.
") } ## Two-factor model fit indices (for comparison - requires SEMLj): ##   cfi.robust   tli.robust rmsea.robust         srmr  ##        1.000        1.000        0.007        0.017  ##  ## Conclusion: The two-factor model fits well (CFI >= 0.95, RMSEA <= 0.06), ##  while the single-factor model does not. The Fit-poor diagnostic correctly ##  invites users to graduate to multi-factor SEM in SEMLj.

title: Latent biomarker constructs and survival
text: lavaan package: Rosseel Y. lavaan: R Package Structural Equation Modeling. J Stat Softw 2012; 48(2): 1 - 36. Package documentation https://lavaan.ugent./. SEMLj: Multi-factor SEM structural paths jamovi. Documentation https://semlj.github.io/. cSEM: Formative composite SEM R. Package documentation https://m-e-rademaker.github.io/cSEM/. seminr: Another R package partial least squares path modelling (formative composites). https://sem--r.github.io/seminr/. title: Interobserver reliability beyond a single kappa
text: reliability study almost never ends one number. report overall Fleiss’ kappa, reviewer asks “two readers actually disagreed?” “diagnostic category dragging agreement ?”, suddenly single summary statistic enough. Interobserver studies structured reporting systems - Yokohama System Reporting Breast cytopathology (YSRB), Milan system, Bethesda system, ISUP grading - routinely pair overall kappa two supplementary tables: Table - every rater pair. Cohen’s kappa (k2)\binom{k}{2} reader pairs, confidence interval significance test. spot outlier reader whose pairwise kappas systematically lower everyone else’s. Table II - every category. per-category agreement rate answers “readers land category c, often agree?” find diagnostic bottleneck - typically “atypical / suspicious” middle category. agreement analysis produces , alongside overall kappa, set rater columns.

title: Interobserver reliability beyond a single kappa
text: real study data redistributable, simulate dataset shape: 99 cases, four readers, five ordinal YSRB categories (= insufficient, II = benign, III = atypical, IV = suspicious, V = malignant) characteristic heavily-benign marginal distribution. First cases (4 readers, YSRB category)
code: library(ClinicoPath)  set.seed(2024) n     <- 99 cats  <- c("I", "II", "III", "IV", "V") prob  <- c(0.05, 0.75, 0.05, 0.04, 0.11)   # mostly benign, as in real cytology truth <- sample(cats, n, replace = TRUE, prob = prob)  # Each reader agrees with the latent truth most of the time, otherwise slips to # an adjacent category. Reader 4 is a little noisier than the rest. slip <- function(x) {   i <- match(x, cats)   cats[pmin(length(cats), pmax(1, i + sample(c(-1, 1), 1)))] } reader <- function(p_agree) {   vapply(truth, function(t) if (runif(1) < p_agree) t else slip(t), character(1)) }  ysrb <- data.frame(   Reader1 = reader(0.92),   Reader2 = reader(0.90),   Reader3 = reader(0.91),   Reader4 = reader(0.84),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) ysrb[] <- lapply(ysrb, factor, levels = cats, ordered = TRUE)  knitr::kable(head(ysrb), caption = "First few cases (4 readers, YSRB category)")

title: Leave-One-Center-Out Cross-Validation
text: leaveonecenterout function performs leave-one-center-cross-validation (LOOCV) internal-external validation multi-institutional prediction models. iteratively holds center test set, trains remaining centers, evaluates predictive performance. implements validation framework recommended TRIPOD guidelines (Debray et al., BMJ 2015). Key features: Three model types: logistic, Cox, linear regression Optional LASSO regularization lambda selection (minimum CV error 1SE rule) Per-center pooled performance metrics (AUC, C-index, R-squared) Forest plot visualization center-specific performance Clinical notices data quality, EPV, discrimination, heterogeneity

title: Leave-One-Center-Out Cross-Validation
text: Two bundled datasets available:
code: library(ClinicoPath) data(loocv_multicenter)  # N=200, 5 centers data(loocv_small)        # N=45, 3 centers

title: Leave-One-Center-Out Cross-Validation
text: Outputs: Study design summary, per-center AUC 95% CI, pooled AUC, forest plot, interpretation heterogeneity assessment.
code: leaveonecenterout(     data = loocv_multicenter,     outcome = "treatment_response",     outcomeLevel = "Responder",     predictors = c("age", "ki67_score", "tumor_size_mm", "grade"),     centerVariable = "institution",     elapsedtime = "os_time",     modelType = "logistic" )

title: Leave-One-Center-Out Cross-Validation
text: Metric: C-index (concordance) 95% CI per center, clamped [0, 1].
code: leaveonecenterout(     data = loocv_multicenter,     outcome = "os_status",     outcomeLevel = "Dead",     predictors = c("age", "ki67_score", "grade"),     centerVariable = "institution",     elapsedtime = "os_time",     modelType = "cox" )

title: Leave-One-Center-Out Cross-Validation
text: Metric: --sample R-squared per center (can negative model predicts worse mean). RMSE also computed.
code: leaveonecenterout(     data = loocv_multicenter,     outcome = "tumor_shrinkage",     outcomeLevel = "Responder",     predictors = c("age", "ki67_score", "tumor_size_mm"),     centerVariable = "institution",     elapsedtime = "os_time",     modelType = "linear" )

title: Leave-One-Center-Out Cross-Validation
text: LASSO (L1 penalty) performs automatic variable selection within CV fold. Recommended number predictors large relative number events.

title: Leave-One-Center-Out Cross-Validation
code: leaveonecenterout(     data = loocv_multicenter,     outcome = "treatment_response",     outcomeLevel = "Responder",     predictors = c("age", "ki67_score", "tumor_size_mm", "ctdna_level",                    "grade", "stage", "gender"),     centerVariable = "institution",     elapsedtime = "os_time",     modelType = "logistic",     useLasso = TRUE,     lambdaMethod = "lambda.1se" )

what: Lambda selection: Minimum CV error (less shrinkage)
title: Leave-One-Center-Out Cross-Validation
code: leaveonecenterout(     data = loocv_multicenter,     outcome = "treatment_response",     outcomeLevel = "Responder",     predictors = c("age", "ki67_score", "tumor_size_mm", "ctdna_level",                    "grade", "stage", "gender"),     centerVariable = "institution",     elapsedtime = "os_time",     modelType = "logistic",     useLasso = TRUE,     lambdaMethod = "lambda.min" )

code: leaveonecenterout(     data = loocv_multicenter,     outcome = "os_status",     outcomeLevel = "Dead",     predictors = c("age", "ki67_score", "tumor_size_mm", "grade"),     centerVariable = "institution",     elapsedtime = "os_time",     modelType = "cox",     useLasso = TRUE )

code: so the principle seems right. you initialise the table in the .init() phase (you add rows and columns), and then you populate the table in the .run() phase. however, i notice your .init() function calls .initcTable() which doesn’t actually do anything. most of the time, .init() isn’t necessary, because the .r.yaml file can take care of it, but sometimes the rows/columns the table should have is a more complex calculation than the .r.yaml allows (and example of this might be the ANOVA table in jmv … there’s not a simple relationship between the number of variables in the option, i.e. dose, supp, and the number of rows in the ANOVA table dose, supp, supp * dose, residuals. so we can’t achieve this with the .r.yaml, and so we set it up in the .init() phase. finally, there are times where you can’t even determine the number of rows/columns in the .init() phase. you can only decide how many rows/columns are appropriate after you’ve run the analysis. an example of this might be a cluster analysis, where there’s a row for each cluster, but you only know how many rows you need after the analysis has been run. this is the least desireable, because it does lead to the growing and shrinking of the table, but sometimes that’s unavoidable. so that’s your order of preference. preferably in the .r.yaml, if that can’t work, then do it in the .init(), and as a last resort, you can do it in the .run()

code: hi, we’ve added “output variables” to version 1.6.16 of jamovi. this allows analyses to save data from the analyses, back to the spreadsheet (for example, residuals). there’s nothing in the 1.6.16 which indicates to users that this functionality is there, and it will only appear when an analysis implements these features. the idea is that we won’t actually release any modules with these features publicly, until an upcoming jamovi 1.8, or 2.0, or whatever. we’ve added these to the 1.6.16 so you can begin developing for the upcoming release. you begin by specifying an output option in your .a.yaml file, i.e.                  # - name: resids                 # title: Residuals                 # type: Output                 # and then add an entry into your .r.yaml file, with a matching name:                 #     - name: resids                 # title: Residuals                 # type: Output                 # varTitle: '`Residuals - ${ dep }`'                 # varDescription: Residuals from ANCOVA                 # clearWith:                 #     - dep                 # - factors                 # - covs                 # - modelTerms                 # in this case you’ll see that i’m specifying a formatted string, where the name of the column produced is generated from the dep variable, or dependent variable.                 # you can populate the output column with:                 #     if (self$options$resids && self$results$resids$isNotFilled()) {                 #         self$results$resids$setValues(aVector)                 #     }                 # sometimes your dataset will have gaps in it, either from filters, or from you calling na.omit() on it, and so if you simply send the residuals from your linear model to $setValues() they won’t be placed in the correct rows. there are two ways to solve this.                 call self$results$resids$setRowNums(...) . conveniently, you can simply take the rownames() from your data set (after calling na.omit()) on it, and pass this in here. i.e.                 # cleanData <- na.omit(self$data)                 # ...                 # rowNums <- rownames(cleanData)                 # self$results$resids$setRowNums(rowNums)                 # alternatively, you can turn your residuals into a data frame, attach the row numbers to that:                 #     residuals <- ...                 # residuals <- data.frame(residuals=residuals, row.names=rownames(cleanData))                 # self$results$setValues(residuals)                 # if you want to provide multiple output columns, for example, perhaps in the previous example we want a “predicted values” column as well, we’d add additional entries to the .a.yaml and the .r.yaml. each entry in the .a.yaml will result in one checkbox.                 # if you want to provide multiple columns with a single checkbox/option, then you can use the items property.                 # - name: predInt                 # title: Prediction intervals                 # varTitle: Pred interval                 # type: Output                 # items: 2                 # then you can go:                 #     self$results$predInt$setValues(index=i, values)                 # or you could wrap both columns of values in a data frame, and go:                 #     self$results$predInt$setValues(valuesinadataframe)                 # you can use data bindings with items too. i.e.                 # - name: resids                 # title: Residuals                 # type: Output                 # varTitle: 'Residuals - $key'                 # items: (vars)                 # this will create an output column for each variable assigned to vars. these can be set:                 #     self$results$resids$setValues(key=key, values)

easyalluvial::add_marginal_histograms(mydata) so you’ve got a few options … but it’s worth pointing out that most of the time, the name of the jamovi function/analysis doesn’t really matter. unless you’re wanting people to be able to use the same functions from R, then no-one will ever use them/see them. (the only thing that matters is that the name of the analysis doesn’t change, so jamovi can match the analysis with analyses in old .omv files) so assuming you want people to be able to use these same functions from R, and you want to rename, say, the flexplota function, you can use rename in the .a.yaml file. we use it for the anova: https://github.com/jamovi/jmv/blob/master/jamovi/anova.a.yaml#L2-L3 this only renames the function used to call the analysis from R, and preserves the underlying ‘analysis name’ that jamovi depends on. in the case of our ANOVA, we decided the lowercase name conflicted with too many anova() functions in R. the only change this makes to your .h.R file is here: https://github.com/jamovi/jmv/blob/master/R/anova.h.R#L527 another approach, if you don’t want to provide the analysis R functions at all, you can see export: false in the .a.yaml file. https://github.com/jamovi/jmv/blob/master/jamovi/empty.a.yaml#L7 in the case of anova, this would completely remove the ANOVA() function from the .h.R file (jamovi doesn’t actually use that top level function itself, rather it constructs the anovaClass, anovaOptions, etc. objects directly) … some times people do this where they want to implement their own top level function, rather than relying on the automatically generated one. or sometimes they just don’t want people to use that function from R, and want them to use a different approach in R. (one usually wants to override the syntax generated for ‘syntax mode’ if taking this approach … i can walk you through that if that’s where you want to head). title: Cure Models for Long-Term Survivors - Comprehensive Guide
text: many solid tumours, proportion patients experience long-term disease-free survival effectively indistinguishable general population. Standard survival models (Cox, Kaplan-Meier) assume every patient eventually experience event, misrepresents prognosis cancers curable subset. Cure models address partitioning population two groups: patients statistically cured patients remain risk (uncured). yields two clinically actionable quantities: cure fraction (probability long-term cure) latency distribution (survival among uncured patients). curemodels module provides four complementary modelling frameworks:

title: Advanced TNM Stage Migration Analysis - Comprehensive Guide
text: new edition AJCC/TNM staging manual released, pathologists oncologists face critical question: revised staging system actually provide better prognostic discrimination one replaces? trivial question. Patients Stage II old criteria may become Stage III new criteria - vice versa. reclassification genuinely separates patients different prognoses, new system improvement. simply reshuffles patients without prognostic benefit, worse, introduces Rogers phenomenon (survival appears improve every stage simply patient reclassification), new system may misleading. stagemigration module provides state---art statistical toolkit answering question. goes far beyond simple cross-tabulation old vs. new stages. analysis includes formal discrimination metrics (Harrell’s C-index), reclassification indices (NRI, IDI), decision curve analysis clinical utility, bootstrap validation internal validity, multiple visualization tools presentations publications. code: set.seed(12345)  # --- Helper functions --- generate_survival_times <- function(stage, hazard_base = 0.02,                                     stage_multipliers = c(1, 1.5, 2.5, 4)) {   stage_numeric <- as.numeric(stage)   hazard <- hazard_base * stage_multipliers[stage_numeric]   times <- rexp(length(stage), rate = hazard) * 12 + rnorm(length(stage), 0, 2)   pmax(times, 0.1) }  generate_censoring <- function(survival_times, censoring_rate = 0.3) {   prob <- pmin(censoring_rate + (survival_times - median(survival_times)) / 100, 0.8)   prob <- pmax(prob, 0.1)   rbinom(length(survival_times), 1, 1 - prob) }  create_stage_migration <- function(old_stage, migration_prob = 0.25) {   new_stage <- as.numeric(old_stage)   n <- length(old_stage)   migrate <- sample(seq_len(n), size = round(n * migration_prob))   for (i in migrate) {     cs <- new_stage[i]     if (cs == 1) new_stage[i] <- sample(c(1, 2, 3), 1, prob = c(0.4, 0.4, 0.2))     else if (cs == 2) new_stage[i] <- sample(1:4, 1, prob = c(0.2, 0.3, 0.3, 0.2))     else if (cs == 3) new_stage[i] <- sample(2:4, 1, prob = c(0.2, 0.4, 0.4))     else new_stage[i] <- sample(3:4, 1, prob = c(0.1, 0.9))   }   factor(new_stage, levels = 1:4,          labels = c("Stage I", "Stage II", "Stage III", "Stage IV")) }  # --- Combined dataset (breast + lung + colorectal, N = 2100) --- make_cohort <- function(n, cancer, hazard_base, mig_prob) {   age <- pmin(pmax(round(rnorm(n, 64, 12)), 30), 90)   sex <- factor(sample(c("Male", "Female"), n, replace = TRUE))   old_num <- sample(1:4, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.28, 0.30, 0.24, 0.18))   old_stage <- factor(old_num, 1:4,                       labels = c("Stage I", "Stage II", "Stage III", "Stage IV"))   new_stage <- create_stage_migration(old_stage, migration_prob = mig_prob)   st <- generate_survival_times(new_stage, hazard_base = hazard_base,                                 stage_multipliers = c(0.7, 1.2, 2.0, 3.5))   ev <- generate_censoring(st, censoring_rate = 0.35)   data.frame(age = age, sex = sex, old_stage = old_stage, new_stage = new_stage,              survival_time = round(st, 1), event = ev, cancer_type = cancer,              stringsAsFactors = FALSE) }  lung_df    <- make_cohort(700, "Lung",       0.015, 0.30) breast_df  <- make_cohort(700, "Breast",     0.008, 0.25) crc_df     <- make_cohort(700, "Colorectal", 0.012, 0.28)  combined_data <- rbind(lung_df, breast_df, crc_df) combined_data$patient_id <- seq_len(nrow(combined_data))  # --- Small sample dataset (N = 50, edge-case testing) --- small_data <- make_cohort(50, "Mixed", 0.015, 0.20)  cat("Combined data:", nrow(combined_data), "patients,",     sum(combined_data$event), "events\n") #> Combined data: 2100 patients, 1155 events cat("Small data:", nrow(small_data), "patients,",     sum(small_data$event), "events\n") #> Small data: 50 patients, 26 events

title: enhancedROC Clinical Readiness Assessment
text: Release Readiness: READY unsupervised clinical use — conditional release possible                 caveats module shows strong foundations: solid statistical implementation using pROC, thoughtful               clinical interpretation text, good warning/notice coverage, publication-ready report sentences.               However, critical issues unimplemented features still visible                 UI (Harrell C-Index, Uno’s C-Statistic, time-dependent ROC, NNT, 14 others),               mathematical issues likelihood ratio handling, missing confidence                 intervals PPV/NPV pathologists clinicians need clinical decision-making.

title: enhancedROC Clinical Readiness Assessment
text: AUC labeling clear: Excellent/Good/Fair/Poor/discrimination categories                   consistent common literature. Context-sensitive guidance: Separate recommendations screening vs. diagnostic                   vs. confirmatory contexts present clinically appropriate. Copy-ready clinical report: .generateClinicalReport() produces Methods                   Results text AUC, 95% CI, sensitivity, specificity, Youden index — exactly needed                   manuscript. Glossary included: Instructions panel glossary Sensitivity, Specificity,                   PPV, NPV, LR+, LR- — appropriate pathologists basic statistics knowledge. Direction auto-detection notice: direction auto-detected, user-visible                   notice explains direction used (e.g., “higher predictor values classify positive”).                   excellent clinical safety. Prevalence adjustment PPV/NPV: option use observed vs. user-specified                   prevalence present notes differences exceed 5%.

title: enhancedROC Clinical Readiness Assessment
text: CRITICAL — AUC interpretation boundary inconsistent: - Instructions panel says AUC                 0.8–0.9 = “Excellent” .interpretAUC() function labels 0.90+ “Excellent”                 0.80-0.89 “Good”. - discrepancy instructions HTML (b.R line 2631-2634)                 actual function (lines 2022-2028) confuse clinicians. MODERATE — Missing confidence intervals PPV NPV: - clinical metrics table                 (clinicalApplicationMetrics) shows PPV NPV point estimates . - clinical use,                 PPV NPV change dramatically prevalence. Clinicians need CIs minimum statement                 prevalence-dependent estimates. - Agresti-Coull Wilson method binomial CIs                 derived metrics (PPV, NPV) implemented. MODERATE — LR+ = Inf reported without explanation: - specificity = 1, LR+ =                 Inf. code (b.R line 1279) correctly flags Inf clinical                 metrics table show Inf without user-friendly label (“Perfect specificity —                 negatives correctly classified”). MINOR — AUC category boundaries differ common guidelines: - Hosmer-Lemeshow                 thresholds used (0.60/0.70/0.80/0.90) one common approach. - Many diagnostic accuracy guidelines                 (STARD, cochrane systematic review guidelines) use 0.70 minimum acceptable threshold. - Consider                 adding footnote indicating classification system used.

Verdict: Mostly correct, minor edge case LR- spec=0

what: 14. Youden Index as Primary Cutoff Method (Lines 931-941)
